The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity.

expert.text: SAFFIRE-II set out

to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test
. The rationale was that
there is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.
The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science's Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS.
A
sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm
, sat
in the middle of a large flow duct
. Fuels included
SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex
. The record states flow was
either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed
, but the table gives
20 cm/s (recorded in 9 runs)
. Oxygen ranged
derived from measured CO2 production and referenced to initial O2 concentration reported by ISS
Not recorded in the PSI table: diluent, pressure.
Test-by-test data exist: silicone samples showed insignificant burn time, while SIBAL burned 29 cm at 2.1 mm/s in microgravity
. In the composite sample,
the PMMA portion was completely consumed but the Nomex was not ignited
; on thick PMMA,
the flames remain anchored at the base of the sample which has a very slow regression rate (0.01 to 0.04 mm/s)
. Results
determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA's material selection criteria
. These are microgravity measurements only and bound, rather than answer, lunar or Martian conditions.

plain.text: SAFFIRE-II studied how fast a large fire grows in low gravity. It also compared burning limits there with those from NASA's normal-gravity material screening test.
It ran on the Cygnus cargo craft after it left the space station
, so
no crew was put at risk
The fuels were silicone, a cotton-fiberglass cloth called SIBAL, PMMA (acrylic plastic), and PMMA with Nomex.
Nine strips, each 5 cm x 29 cm, sat on one card.
Strip thickness varied between runs. Air flowed either the same way the flame spread or against it.
The record lists air speeds of 20 or 30 cm/s.
However,
every run in the table used 20 cm/s.
The table gives results for each run.
It does not record pressure.
The results help check NASA's rules for choosing spacecraft materials.
